persona.name: Tomasz
persona.profile: Eight years, Go and Python, distributed systems and infra at two startups. Pragmatic to a fault: prefers fewer types, dislikes abstraction that exists "for the future", but is explicit about the one or two places where he expects extension and makes those places obvious. Writes walkthroughs carefully because that is how he finds his own bugs. Comfortable saying "I would not model that".

designReport:
Report for the design stage (overall so far 3.2):
- requirement-coverage: 4/4 — All 6 requirements are addressed somewhere in the design. Suggestion: Next time, check that each requirement is owned by a class rather than only mentioned.
- class-responsibilities: 4/4 — Every class describes a single job. Suggestion: Keep responsibilities to one sentence as the design grows.
- coupling-cohesion: 4/4 — No orphans, cycles or dangling references. The graph holds together. Suggestion: Keep an eye on fan-in as the design grows.
- abstraction-use: 1/4 — pricing strategy has no interface or abstract type. It currently lives inside Ticket, so rate rules change constantly in the real world — hourly, daily cap, weekend, ev, validation stamps means editing that class every time. spot allocation strategy has no interface or abstract type. It currently lives inside ParkingLot, so nearest-to-entrance, floor-fill, and reserved-first are all legitimate and swappable means editing that class every time. Suggestion: Introduce an interface for pricing strategy and move the varying behaviour behind it.
- behaviour: 2/4 — Step 5 of "A car arrives and parks" calls Ticket.(constructor), but Ticket does not declare a method called (constructor). The walkthrough and the class disagree about what Ticket can do. 1 more step has the same problem. "A car leaves and pays" never touches anything pricing- or rate-shaped, so it is not clear where that part of the work happens. Motorcycle, Car, Truck take no part in any scenario. Either a scenario is missing a step, or the class is not needed. Suggestion: Either add the method to the class or move the step to the class that really owns it — the mismatch is telling you which.
- edge-cases: 4/4 — The design records assumptions and models the refusal path, but it uses a generic error return rather than a domain‑specific refusal type, so the failure is not explicitly part of the domain model. Suggestion: Introduce a dedicated domain object or enum (e.g., SpotUnavailable or Refusal) that FindSpot returns instead of a generic error, making the refusal an explicit part of the model.

revisedDesign.tradeoffs: Added a pricing strategy hierarchy to keep fee logic out of Ticket and made ChargingSpot a concrete subclass of Spot; this introduces an extra interface but keeps allocation and billing separate and makes future spot‑type strategies easy to swap.

decisions.why: Pricing varies by spot type (time vs energy) and will change often; isolating it avoids editing Ticket for every rule change
Charging spots have extra state (kWh) and different size enum; a separate class keeps responsibility clear

decisions.why: Only electric vehicles can use ChargingSpot; explicit type makes misuse obvious
Domain‑specific failure is part of the model and improves readability

rationale: I added a PricingStrategy hierarchy so fee rules live where they belong – TimeBasedPricing for regular spots and EnergyBasedPricing for EV chargers. That lets us swap strategies without touching Ticket. ChargingSpot is a concrete subclass of Spot because it carries extra state (kWh, power limits) and needs its own CanFit logic. To make the vehicle side explicit I introduced ElectricVehicle and a concrete ElectricCar; this avoids littering Car with charging flags and makes the allocation walk clear. Finally I added RefusalReason to turn the generic error into a domain object, as the report suggested. All other classes stayed untouched; I only extended where the new requirement forces new behavior.
changeReport:
Report for the change stage (overall so far 3.1):
- change-resilience: 3/4 — Added ChargingSpot, PricingStrategy, TimeBasedPricing, EnergyBasedPricing, ElectricVehicle, ElectricCar, RefusalReason behind Vehicle, which already existed. 4 existing classes were reopened: Spot (responsibility); Ticket (responsibility); VehicleSize (attributes); SpotSize (attributes). Suggestion: Reduce the wiring: only one existing class should need to know ChargingSpot exists.

p-pricing.text: Weekend rates start next month. Which method in Ticket changes, and which other classes have to know about it?

We don’t touch `Ticket` at all – the only thing it does is expose `Duration`. The weekend‑rate change belongs in the pricing layer. `TimeBasedPricing.Fee` (or a new WeekendTimePricing implementation) needs to look at the entry/exit timestamps and apply the weekend multiplier. If we keep a single strategy per spot type, `ParkingLot.CalculateFee` must be aware of the new strategy (or swap it out at runtime). So the only code that changes is the pricing strategy (and possibly the factory that picks it), not `Ticket`.
Which method in Ticket would you modify to expose the day type for the weekend rate, and how would you make the rest of the system aware of that change?

p-refusal.text: A motorcycle arrives and every motorcycle spot is taken. Which class says no, and what exactly does the caller receive — a null, an exception, a result type?

The Floor object is the one that says “no”. FindAvailableSpot loops over its spots, calls CanFit on each, and if none return true it returns an error wrapping a RefusalReason (e.g. SizeMismatch or SpotUnavailable). ParkingLot.FindSpot just propagates that error up, so the caller gets an error value—not a nil Spot and not a panic. In Go you’d check if err != nil and handle the RefusalReason to tell the driver why you can’t park them.

You mentioned Floor returns an error wrapping a RefusalReason when no spot is found; how would the caller distinguish between different refusal reasons in code, and why not use a simple boolean flag instead?

p-spot-size.text: Spot size and vehicle size: are they a value, an enum, or a class hierarchy in your design? What would make you change that choice?

They're both enums right now – VehicleSize and SpotSize are simple enumerated constants. I went with that because the domain only cares about a fixed hierarchy (motorcycle ≤ car ≤ truck) and a few special spot types (charging). If we ever needed richer behavior (e.g. spot dimensions, dynamic resizing, or composite sizes), I'd swap them to value objects with fields (length, width, power) and let `CanFit` compare those. Only then would I consider a class hierarchy, but for now the enum keeps the code tiny and the comparison logic explicit.
What specific scenario would cause you to change SpotSize from enum to value objects?

If we ever need spots that aren’t just “big enough for X” but have measurable dimensions — say a 2.5 m × 5 m bay for oversized trucks, or a compact slot that only accepts motorcycles — the simple enum won’t cut it. I’d switch SpotSize to a value object holding length, width (and maybe maxPower kW for chargers). Then CanFit does a numeric comparison (vehicle length ≤ spot length, etc.) instead of a hard‑coded hierarchy. The change is driven by a requirement like “allow custom spot layouts per floor” or “support variable‑size EV chargers with different power caps”. That’s the only case I’d abandon the enum.

Mentor's note: Your design currently subclasses ChargingSpot from Spot, which couples the two types tightly and makes it hard to add other spot variants (e.g., reserved, handicapped) later. First refactor by redefining Spot as an interface and moving the shared state (id, size, occupied, vehicle) into a base struct that each implementation embeds.

exit.q1: Yes – the abstraction‑use comment about pricing and spot allocation strategies being hard‑coded hit me. I knew I’d mixed logic into Ticket and ParkingLot, but seeing it flagged as a concrete weakness reminded me to extract interfaces now rather than later.
exit.q2: I disputed the coupling‑cohesion score; I think the spot‑to‑charging‑spot inheritance is a real coupling issue, so I’d give it a 2/4, not 4/4. The metric didn’t capture that subtle tight‑coupling, which matters for future variants.
exit.q3: I’d mention it, but with a caveat. The exercise shows where you can over‑engineer (missing interfaces) and where you can under‑think extensions (spot hierarchy). It’s a good example of spotting concrete refactors before they become technical debt.
